name: Conservative democracy
summary: Conservative democracy (muhafazakâr demokrasi) is the political identity Turkey's Justice and Development Party (AKP) adopted after 2002 to mark its break with the Islamist National Outlook tradition. It presents conservatism as gradual change that keeps 'perennial' values (family, religion as a social value, national culture) inside a democratic, pluralist and rule-of-law framework: legitimacy rests on the will of the people, secularism means the state's impartiality towards all beliefs rather than hostility to religion, politics is a realm of compromise, and the economy is a market economy with a social state. Its programme sought EU membership, civilian control of the military and wider cultural rights.
scope: As the defining scholarship sets it out: Çağlıyan-İçener (Turkish Studies 2009) treats conservative democracy as the AKP's self-defining concept, formulated by its leaders and theorist Yalçın Akdoğan and resting on the party programme; Kaddorah (ACRPS 2015) and Aslan (AJISS 2013) analyse it from the party's programme, Akdoğan's writings and the 2012 'Political Vision of AK Parti 2023', which opens with a section on the 'conservative democrat political identity'. The profile is answered from that scholarship, the AKP programme (2001) and the 2012 Political Vision. As the doctrine of a party that governed alone, its record counts too: the acts of AKP governments up to 2012 as the Vision and Çağlıyan-İçener report them answer statements on their own (record over words). Erdoğan's later rule (post-2013, the 2017 presidential system), which the scholarship treats under other labels such as Erdoğanism and which these defining sources do not document, is not covered; nor are critics' readings of a 'hidden agenda'. Conservatism and democracy in general, and the US 'Conservative Democrats', are other subjects.
